outcomes: Chooses between a developing move and a non-developing move without being told which kind each is
Names the concrete job that makes a rook-pawn move right: it attacks a pinning piece, takes a square or stops a plan
Sees when the same pawn move simply costs time

steps.text: **Moves that help and moves that wait** sorted moves into helping and waiting. Now you choose with no label. A rook-pawn move (a move of the a- or h-pawn) is rarely best, and it is right when it has a concrete job: it attacks a piece that pins, takes a square the opponent wants, or stops a plan. *Rule of thumb:* ask what the pawn will attack, then compare it with the best developing move.

The job has to be real. A pin does not make every pawn move the best one: compare it with the developing moves. And a plan has to be a plan the opponent can carry out. If you cannot name what the pawn attacks, it is a waiting move, and waiting moves cost time when the opponent can use it.

steps.title: Does the pawn have a job?
steps.prompt: A rook-pawn move aimed at a pinning bishop in two positions. Predict whether it is the best choice in each.
Think of the last rook-pawn move you played in an opening. What did the pawn attack? If you cannot say, what would you play instead?
